outcomes.question: Before I put time into this: is it well regarded? Has it been criticised or superseded?
outcomes.text:
It's well regarded enough to have won the 2025 Berggruen essay prize [spya-gp3g6s]. It has also drawn replies, including [a Noema rebuttal by Barton Friedland, as described in this post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/pevansgreenwood_the-consciences-debate-continues-in-noema-activity-7443091909155270656-CJZ2) and [a Medium critique](https://medium.com/@Lidinwise/why-the-mythology-of-conscious-ai-misses-the-deeper-point-437589461d45). I found nothing saying it's been superseded.

outcomes.question: What should I read before or alongside this to get the most out of it?
outcomes.text:
Read the essay first, then pair it with a critic, which suits a reading group. Two replies take on his central moves: [Why I am not a biological naturalist](https://philarchive.org/archive/DUNWIA-4) and [Contra Anil Seth](https://www.againstmoloch.com/writing/2026-03-18_contraAnilSethOnAIConsciousness.html). Before you start, read where he names the assumption he attacks [spya-wepmnr].

Is your group more interested in the philosophy or the ethics?

outcomes.question: Who is the author, and how far should I trust them on this subject?
outcomes.text:
Seth directs Sussex's Centre for Consciousness Science [spya-rg493b], so he is well placed on the subject. But the essay leans on his own predictive-processing view, which critics call [too vague to pin down consciousness](https://philosophymindscience.org/index.php/phimisci/article/download/9153/8691). He admits his view is a minority one [spya-qu7j89].

outcomes.text:
It's influential but openly partisan, so read it as advocacy. Gwern's own follow-up, [Scaling Hypothesis Revisited](https://gwern.net/scaling-hypothesis-revisited), is also pointed to in the piece [spya-ewxv9q]. Critics include a [philosophy-of-science paper](https://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/23622/1/psa_scaling_hypothesis_manuscript.pdf) on whether the strong version can be tested, and a [Hacker News thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=31564033) doubting the extrapolation.

outcomes.question: Who is the author, and how far should I trust them on this subject?
outcomes.text:
Gwern Branwen is an independent writer. His [Google Scholar page](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=yk1QMowAAAAJ&hl=en) lists him as independent, with no institution. The search turned up no credentials or outside assessments, so I can't say how far to trust him from it.

The essay is an advocate's argument. He says he was wrong to doubt scaling [spya-emqjaa], and he attacks the experts who disagreed [spya-zyncdd]. For your group, check his predictions against what happened afterward. He wrote a [2022 follow-up](https://gwern.net/scaling-hypothesis-revisited) that is a good place to start.

outcomes.question: Before I put time into this: is it well regarded? Has it been criticised or superseded?
outcomes.text:
It's widely discussed, and it's contested. The strong claim is the disputed part. A [philosophy-of-science paper](https://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/23622/1/psa_scaling_hypothesis_manuscript.pdf) says it is hard to test because it never says in advance which abilities will emerge or when. A [LesswRong commenter](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/XusDPpXr6FYJqWkxh/an-156-the-scaling-hypothesis-a-plan-for-building-agi) says it doesn't show scaling will work in practice. Gwern wrote a [followup in 2022](https://gwern.net/scaling-hypothesis-revisited). Worth reading, but as an argument to test.
